notes.meaning: Jesus travelled south toward Judea and crossed over the Jordan River into the region of Perea. Large crowds gathered around Him again, and He welcomed them and taught them as He always did. Sharing God's truth was His regular practice wherever He went.

Some Pharisees came up and asked Jesus whether a man is allowed to divorce his wife. They were not looking for honest guidance, but trying to trap Him into saying something unpopular or unlawful. The local ruler, Herod Antipas, had recently executed John the Baptist for speaking out against an unlawful marriage.

Jesus answered their test by asking what the law of Moses told them to do. The religious leaders replied that Moses allowed a man to write a divorce certificate and send his wife away. They treated this legal permission as if God approved of ending a marriage for almost any reason.

Jesus explained that Moses wrote this rule only because the people had stubborn and hard hearts. The certificate of divorce was meant to limit cruelty and protect wives from being cast out with no rights. It was a concession to human weakness rather than God's original standard.

Jesus pointed them back to the very beginning when God created the world. God designed humanity from the start as male and female to fit together in marriage. His true plan for family life goes back long before Moses gave legal regulations.

Quoting Genesis, Jesus explained that marriage creates a bond closer than the relationship between parents and children. A husband and wife are joined together so completely that God counts them as one flesh. They are no longer two separate lives, but one shared life that is meant to last.

Because God Himself unites a husband and wife in marriage, no human being should pull them apart. Marriage is not merely a social contract, but a sacred union established by the Creator. Breaking that bond works directly against what God intended.

Once they were back inside a house, the disciples asked Jesus more questions about marriage and divorce. He often used quiet moments indoors to explain difficult lessons away from the crowds. The disciples realized that His standard was far higher than the common customs of their day.

Jesus told them that whoever divorces a spouse and marries another person commits adultery against the original partner. God designed marriage to last for life, so setting aside a spouse to take someone else breaks faith with the marriage bond. Jesus applied this truth equally to both husbands and wives.

differ.view: Remarriage is allowed when divorce occurs because of marital unfaithfulness or abandonment by an unbelieving spouse.
Marriage forms an unbreakable bond until death, so any remarriage while a former spouse is still alive is adultery.

notes.meaning: Parents and guardians brought young children to Jesus so He would place His hands on them and pray for them. The disciples scolded the people and tried to turn them away, thinking children were an unnecessary distraction. Those who brought the children believed that Christ's blessing would do their souls good.

Jesus was indignant when He saw His disciples turning the children away, and He commanded them to stop. He welcomed the young ones openly and stated that God's kingdom belongs to people like them. Children are never too small or insignificant to receive the Lord's care.

differ.view: Infants can belong to the kingdom of God and should be brought to Christ in baptism, where God creates faith.
Children of believers are included in God's covenant promises and receive infant baptism as a sign of Christ's welcome.
Christ's loving reception of young children provides strong warrant for bringing infants to holy baptism.
This passage describes Jesus blessing children rather than baptising them, since baptism requires conscious, personal faith in Christ.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Jesus' tender care for children supports the hopeful trust that God provides a way of salvation for infants who die without baptism.

notes.meaning: Jesus declared that no one can enter God's kingdom without receiving it like a little child. Children do not attempt to earn gifts, but simply accept what they are given with humble trust. People must lay aside pride and receive God's kingdom as a free gift of grace.

Jesus scooped the children into His arms, laid His hands on their heads, and blessed them warmly. He did not simply tolerate them, but showed genuine tenderness and delight in their presence. His action showed how deeply God values the humble and weak.

A wealthy young leader ran up and knelt before Jesus with great eagerness and respect. He asked what good work he needed to do in order to inherit eternal life, meaning everlasting life with God. Although he was earnest, he mistakenly viewed salvation as a reward to be earned by human effort.

Jesus asked the man why he called Him good, noting that only God possesses absolute goodness. He was not denying His own divinity, but challenging the man to consider who Jesus really is. The man needed to measure goodness by God's perfect character rather than mere human standards.

Jesus cited several commandments from the law of Moses that focus on how we treat our neighbors. He mentioned murder, adultery, stealing, lying, cheating, and honoring parents so the man could evaluate his own life. True love for God always produces fair and honest treatment of other people.

The man replied that he had kept all these rules ever since he was a young boy. He answered sincerely, but he evaluated himself only by outward behavior rather than the deeper obedience of the heart. He felt he had lived a moral life, yet his conscience still felt that something was missing.

Jesus looked at the man with deep love and pointed out the one thing he still lacked. He told him to sell his possessions, give the proceeds to the poor, and follow Him, promising him treasure in heaven. This was not a universal command for all believers, but a direct test that exposed how much this man loved his wealth above God.

The man's face fell in dark gloom at these words, and he walked away full of grief. His great wealth was his idol, and he was unwilling to let go of it to follow Christ. His departure showed the sorrow of choosing earthly riches over eternal life.

Jesus looked around at His followers and explained how hard it is for wealthy people to enter God's kingdom. Wealth tends to create self-reliance and false security, blinding people to their spiritual poverty. Possessions easily become a trap that keeps the heart from turning to God.

The disciples were shocked, because people in their culture assumed that wealth was a clear sign of God's special favor. Jesus addressed them tenderly as children, but He did not weaken His warning. He repeated that entering the kingdom of God is extraordinarily difficult for those who rely on earthly riches.

Jesus used an extreme word picture to show that entering the kingdom is humanly impossible for the wealthy. He stated that it is easier for a camel to squeeze through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom. Trusting in possessions makes it impossible for someone to humble themselves before God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular explanation claims the needle's eye was a small night gate in Jerusalem's wall where a camel had to kneel and be unloaded to pass through.

notes.meaning: The disciples were utterly astonished and asked among themselves who could possibly be saved. If the rich, who seemed to have every blessing and advantage, could not enter, ordinary people seemed to have no chance at all. Their question showed they still needed to learn that salvation is a gift from God, not something humans can achieve on their own.
